Fixes bug if new processes resumes first

When we fork/clone, the new process might start its execution first (and
tracer sees it get a SIGTRAP). In this case, we wait for the fork call
to return before we insert things into the database and resume it
(previously, a unknown process would be created for it, plus a duplicate
when fork actually returned. That was bad).

Handles symbolic links at the 'trace' step

Previously, only the symlink itself would be considered, assigned to a
package and written to the configuration. The 'pack' step would then see
the links that the path traverses, and the final target, and pack them
with the link.

This was wrong, because a symlink's target can come from a package
itself, and the fact that these files were to be handled separately
without appearing in the configuration posed other problems (when
unpacking).

The tracer now adds the symlinks and targets to the list of files to the
list of files that is read from the database. They still don't appear
there, but are in the configuration from the start. They will be
categorized in the packages, and other steps do not need to worry about
them (if a symlink appears in the configuration, we can just assume that
the target is also listed).

Use PTRACE_EVENT_EXEC instead of syscall return

Previously, I was relying on the syscall-return-stop out of execve() to
detect that an exec had happened. This had a number of drawbacks:
* Can't be sure which thread executed (although race conditions here are
  not common)
* Need to read orig_eax on syscall-return-stop to know which syscall we
  are returning from, although in normal circumstances we should know
  (it's the one we entered). Also, that value might apparently be set
  wrong...
* Needed to work around i386/x86_64 transitions, as Linux could report a
  thread going out of "syscall 59", number for execve in x86_64,
  although the new program is running in i386 mode

We now react to PTRACE_EVENT_EXEC and do the work there. We then set the
flag PROCFLAG_EXECD, so that we know the next syscall-in/out-stop is in
fact a return from execve, no matter what Linux reports (and whether or
not the thread had entered a syscall before).

Use PTRACE_EVENT_FORK, ... instead of syscall out

Previously, I was only using the syscall-return-stop out of fork(),
vfork() or clone() to detect that a successful process creation had
happened. This was a problem because syscall return can happen either
before or after the process is created.

* When we return first, we created a new PROCSTAT_ALLOCATED that will be
  seen later (then options get set and it turns into PROCSTAT_ATTACHED).
* When it appears first, an unknown process was created in
  PROCSTAT_UNKNOWN and stays STOPped until the syscall returns, set it
  to it to PROCSTAT_ATTACHED and resumed it.

This was already a workaround, but worked. Problem is that vfork()
doesn't actually return before the new process appeared and run until it
dies or calls execve(), which couldn't happen because the syscall
resumes it; this meant deadlock on any vfork() call.

We now react to PTRACE_EVENT_{FORK,VFORK,CLONE} instead, which always
happens before the new process appears. We can get rid of the two
different handling depending on the random order chosen by the kernel,
and vfork won't deadlock anymore.

PERF: Allow compiler to choose best way to construct a copy

With move semantics added to the language and the standard library updated with
move constructors added for many types it is now interesting to take an
argument directly by value, instead of by const-reference, and then copy. This
check allows the compiler to take care of choosing the best way to construct
the copy.

The transformation is usually beneficial when the calling code passes an rvalue
and assumes the move construction is a cheap operation. This short example
illustrates how the construction of the value happens:

class Foo {
 public:
-  Foo(const std::string &Copied, const std::string &ReadOnly)
-    : Copied(Copied), ReadOnly(ReadOnly) {}
+  Foo(std::string Moved, const std::string &ReadOnly)
+    : Copied(std::move(Moved)), ReadOnly(ReadOnly) {}
 private:
   private:
   std::string Copied;
   const std::string &ReadOnly;
};

STYLE: Use range-based loops from C++11

Used as a more readable equivalent to the traditional for loop operating
over a range of values, such as all elements in a container, in the
forward direction.

====
Range based loopes are more explicit for only computing the
end location once for containers.

for ( ImageIORegion::IndexType::const_iterator i = this->GetIndex().begin();
  i != this->GetIndex().end(); //<- NOTE: Compute end every loop iteration
  ++i )

for (long i : this->GetIndex()) //<- NOTE: Implicitly only compute end once

====
Explicitly reduce the amount of index computations: (The compiler
probably does this too)

for(int i = 0; i < 11; i++)
  {
  pos[0] = testPoints[i][0];
  pos[1] = testPoints[i][1];
                    ^^^^

for(auto & testPoint : testPoints)
  {

STYLE: Prefer C++11 type alias over typedef

== http://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/type_alias ==

Type alias is a name that refers to a previously defined type (similar
to typedef).

A type alias declaration introduces a name which can be used as a
synonym for the type denoted by type-id. It does not introduce a new
type and it cannot change the meaning of an existing type name. There is
no difference between a type alias declaration and typedef declaration.
This declaration may appear in block scope, class scope, or namespace
scope.

== https://www.quora.com/Is-using-typedef-in-C++-considered-a-bad-practice ==

While typedef is still available for backward compatibility, the new
Type Alias syntax 'using Alias = ExistingLongName;' is more consistent
with the flow of C++ than the old typedef syntax 'typedef
ExistingLongName Alias;', and it also works for templates (Type alias,
alias template (since C++11)), so leftover 'typedef' aliases will differ
in style from any alias templates.

https://stackoverflow.com/questions/39932391/virtual-override-or-both-c

When you override a function you don't technically need to write either virtual
or override.

The original base class declaration needs the keyword virtual to mark it as virtual.

In the derived class the function is virtual by way of having the ¹same type as
the base class function.

However, an override can help avoid bugs by producing a compilation error when
the intended override isn't technically an override. E.g. that the function
type isn't exactly like the base class function. Or that a maintenance of the
base class changes that function's type, e.g. adding a defaulted argument.

In the same way, a virtual keyword in the derived class can make such a bug
more subtle, by ensuring that the function is still is virtual in further
derived classes.

So the general advice is,

virtual for the base class function declaration.
This is technically necessary.

Use override (only) for a derived class' override.
This helps with maintenance.

Add initial disabled nullable directive

Nullable reference types are a way of annotating types that can or cannot be null. It's a new feature added in C# 8.0 that can drastically limit the number of null reference exceptions in a running app. Since many of the issues in deployment have been around uncaught nulls, it makes sense to set the project up to enable them.

It's quite daunting to add them to a code base at one time, so the general pattern is to turn it on globally, then turn them off for each page. This change accomplishes that. Future changes can then handle enabling them on a class-by-class basis. An effect of this change is that any new classes will be forced to handle nullable reference types, which limits new code from introducing null reference exceptions.

Add initial disabled nullable directive (#232)

Nullable reference types are a way of annotating types that can or cannot be null. It's a new feature added in C# 8.0 that can drastically limit the number of null reference exceptions in a running app. Since many of the issues in deployment have been around uncaught nulls, it makes sense to set the project up to enable them.

It's quite daunting to add them to a code base at one time, so the general pattern is to turn it on globally, then turn them off for each page. This change accomplishes that. Future changes can then handle enabling them on a class-by-class basis. An effect of this change is that any new classes will be forced to handle nullable reference types, which limits new code from introducing null reference exceptions.

user can change default settings in loop file

User can now change 3 different default settings in the loop file:

1) Using the STEP command a user can change the step sizes during
differentiation for the various parameters.
example: This would change the default step size for dihedral FC to 0.1
DIR ./
READ mm3.fld
STEP df 0.1
[...]

2) Max number of parameters used during simplex optimization
example: This would change the maxiumum parameters used for simplex optimization to 5.
[...]
CDAT [...]
RDAT [...]
COMP
LOOP 0.01
GRAD
SIMP max_params=5
END

3) Control gradient optimization methods. The user can turn on or off various optimizers, along
with changing the cutoff, radii, and factor values. Users should know what these values do
before changing the default settings.
example: This would turn off SVD, ensure lstsq is used with cutoffs between 0.1-10.0, and ensure legrange is used with four different factors and three different radii and no cutoffs.
[...]
CDAT [...]
RDAT [...]
COMP
LOOP 0.01
GRAD lstsq=True,cutoff[0.1/10.0] SVD=False legrange=True,factor[0.01/0.1/1.0/10.0],radii[0.01/0.2/5.0],cutoff[None]

relativly inclusive matching pattern. Two examples are for the
Heck reaction and the osmium dihydroxylation reaction. When
matching the alkene with the substrucutre (C2=C2-00) an aromatic
group would be matched which would give (in the case of benzene)
3 matches for double bonds, with four different matches per bond
giving a total of 12 additional structures. This code iterates
through the rings and matches to determine those matches that
are within the ring (2+ atoms in both matches and the ring) and
then determines if it is aromatic or not.

Also the code would prevent structures that are intended to have
multiple matches such as (2,1,5) and (5,1,2) to use both matches.
To fix this I added logic to determine if the 'b_cs_first_match_only'
is true before determinig if the matches are unique or not.

Changed how parameter step sizes are modified.

Parameter step sizes are used during parameter differentiation.
In central differentiation, we often want to prevent parameters
from reaching negative values. If a paramter was not allowed to
go below zero, and the new_value,

    new_value = old_value - step_size,

reached a negative value, the step size would be modified to

    new_step_size = old_value * 0.1.

In this sense, the parameter could never go below zero because its
maximum decrease would be 1/10th of its current value.

However, this method doesn't work for preventing parameters from
exceeding some maximum value. In this commit, we use a new algorithm
to determine new step sizes, as follows:

    upper_allowed_range = abs(old_value - max_allowed_value)
    lower_allowed_range = abs(old_value - min_allowed_value)
    min_allowed_range = min(upper_allowed_range, lower_allowed_range)
    new_step_size = min_allowed_range * 0.1

This will produce the same result when preventing parameters from going
below zero, but should also work to prevent parameters from exceeding
certain thresholds.

The code used to check if lines and self.lines was None, however, self.lines is
now actually a property. When self.lines was updated to being a property, this
negatively affected that behavior.

For example, if you were to say

    if self.lines is None:
        do_stuff()

This would actually call upon the property self.lines. This property looks like
this

    @property
    def lines(self):
        if self._lines is None:
            with open(self.path, 'r') as f:
                self._lines = f.readlines()
        return self._lines
    @lines.setter
    def lines(self, x):
        self._lines = x

This means that you can call upon self.lines, it will check if self._lines is
None. If it is, then it attempts to read the lines. This would cause problems
when self.path was also None because it couldn't open the file to read the
lines.

Basically, self.lines was being called when self.path was None, which resulted
in errors.

Better python2/3 compatabilities, coding styles

- I've gone through the code and edited a lot of places to adopt a cleaner
  style to make the code compatible with python 2 and 3
- Most of these changes are based on suggestions from
  https://portingguide.readthedocs.io/en/latest/index.html
- In a lot of places python2 will now be using lists where iterators were
  used before. This is due to a major shift in python 3 where iterators
  are now a bigger focus. In all likelyhood this won't cause any significant
  loss in performance unless the iterables contain many thousands of objects
- Using the built-in methods which return lists in python 2 and iterators in
  python 3 keeps the codebase smaller, more readable, and avoids external
  dependencies
- Below are explanations for major changes to coding style along with
  explanations of the changes in behavior from python 2 to 3 and preferred
  styles to use in the future to keep the code compatible with both versions
- Keep in mind that python 2 is end-of-life in 2020 and Schrodinger has
  switched to only support python 3 since any release 2018 or later, so
  using python 3 now is encouraged

Iterators no longer have .next(), use next()

- In python 3 the .next() method was removed from iterators
- Instead the next() built-in method should be used, i.e. next(iterator)
- next() built-in was backported to python 2.6+ so this should be fine
- One note is that according to Schrodinger's python API reference, I believe that the structure.StructureReader
  still relies on .next() through their 2018u3 release. In 2018u4 their documentation of this changes to use next()
  so for the time being I have left this to use .next() since the CRC currently only has 2018u3. You can find the reference
  to StructureReader for 2018u3 and 2018u4 at
  http://content.schrodinger.com/Docs/r2018-3/python_api/api/schrodinger.structure.html#schrodinger.structure.StructureReader
  and
  http://content.schrodinger.com/Docs/r2018-4/python_api/api/schrodinger.structure.html#schrodinger.structure.StructureReader

Use absolute imports and explicit relative imports

- In python3 absolute imports are checked first before implicit relative imports
- In python2 this was the other way around, so if your module had a submodule names math, then `import math` would import that submodule rather than the module from the standard library
- Add `from __future__ import absolute_import` to bring this behavior to python2
- Absolute imports used for core python modules
- Submodules imported from q2mm or other python modules should use absolute import syntax or atleast explicit relative syntax
- E.g. `import q2mm.gradient` or `import .gradient` are ok but not `import gradient` when importing q2mm's gradient submodule

Use python3 division to result in float

- In python3, division of two ints results in a float
- In python2, this resulted in an int instead
- Use `from __future__ import division` to bring python3 division behavior to python2
- If you desire the old behavior, use `//` as the division operator to return an int
- I've done some preliminary checks and didn't see any obvious places where the int was needed without explicitly being typed
- If anything breaks, please keep this change in mind if your code uses any division

Changing instances of map() to list comprehension

- In python3 map() now returns an iterator instead of a list
- I've exchanged cases where a list was needed with list comprehensions
- I tried to leave map() in places where an iterator would still work
- In the future use list comprehensions when you need a list, or map
when you need an iterator
- Wrapping map in list (i.e. list(map(func, iterable))) is OK but not
very pythonic

Changing izip() to zip()

- In python3 zip() now generates an iterator where in python2 izip() from itertools was needed to do this.
- Previously I changed these to use zip() if python3 was being used or izip() if python2 was being used
- In favor of readability and removing unnecessary dependencies I've changed all of these to just use zip() regardless of python version
- This is highly unlikely to cause any significant problems with performance

Changing xrange() to range()

- In python3 range() now behave exactly how xrange() did in python2
- Most likely this won't affect performance anywhere, so for readability just using range()

Changing any dict.iter*() to dict.*()

- In python3 dict.iteritems(), dict.iterkeys(), etc. has been removed
- Similarly dict.viewitems(), etc. has also been removed
- Instead dict.items(), etc. now returns a view object
- Views are memory efficient like iterators but are dynamic in that
  changing the dictionary changes what is in the view
- For the most part, when iterating over the keys or values in a dict
  it will work the same as iterating over lists unless the dict object
  is changed

Leaving version switch to deal with basestring

- Basestring has been removed from python3 as all text-type strings
  are now unicode, which was not the case in python2
- Most solutions to this require dependence on `six` or another python
  module for dealing with python2/3 differences in a clean way
- Since most of these compatabilities have been handled without using
  an external dependence then to avoid adding that dependence I'm just
  going to leave the if statements which switch behavior based on
  python version

Correcting behavior of SVD

See the discussion on issue #28 for more details. I will try to
recap some because this discussion will unfortunately not transfer
to forked repositories of Q2MM.

SVD should do the following.

    J = U . s . V
    x = VT . s' . (UT . r)

Captial T stands for transpose. s' is a modified version of s. J is
the Jacobian and r is the residual vector.

As described by Per-Ola, "The beauty of it is that, since you don't
invert the small values, but set the inverse equal to zero
(counter-intuitive), you get rid of linear dependencies between
parameters, and all parameters with only small influence on the
objective function."

With the modification in this commit, I use np.linalg.svd where the
argument full_matrices is set to False. This is the only way I could
get the matrix multiplication to work with the above formula.

However, there is commented out code for using the full matrices,
which of course fails when you attempt to solve for the parameter
changes, x.

Previously, the code did this.

    A = JT . J
    b = JT . r
    A = U . s . V
    A' = U . s' . V
    A' . x = b

Better python2/3 compatabilities, coding styles (#49)

- I've gone through the code and edited a lot of places to adopt a cleaner
  style to make the code compatible with python 2 and 3
- Most of these changes are based on suggestions from
  https://portingguide.readthedocs.io/en/latest/index.html
- In a lot of places python2 will now be using lists where iterators were
  used before. This is due to a major shift in python 3 where iterators
  are now a bigger focus. In all likelyhood this won't cause any significant
  loss in performance unless the iterables contain many thousands of objects
- Using the built-in methods which return lists in python 2 and iterators in
  python 3 keeps the codebase smaller, more readable, and avoids external
  dependencies
- Below are explanations for major changes to coding style along with
  explanations of the changes in behavior from python 2 to 3 and preferred
  styles to use in the future to keep the code compatible with both versions
- Keep in mind that python 2 is end-of-life in 2020 and Schrodinger has
  switched to only support python 3 since any release 2018 or later, so
  using python 3 now is encouraged

Iterators no longer have .next(), use next()

- In python 3 the .next() method was removed from iterators
- Instead the next() built-in method should be used, i.e. next(iterator)
- next() built-in was backported to python 2.6+ so this should be fine
- One note is that according to Schrodinger's python API reference, I believe that the structure.StructureReader
  still relies on .next() through their 2018u3 release. In 2018u4 their documentation of this changes to use next()
  so for the time being I have left this to use .next() since the CRC currently only has 2018u3. You can find the reference
  to StructureReader for 2018u3 and 2018u4 at
  http://content.schrodinger.com/Docs/r2018-3/python_api/api/schrodinger.structure.html#schrodinger.structure.StructureReader
  and
  http://content.schrodinger.com/Docs/r2018-4/python_api/api/schrodinger.structure.html#schrodinger.structure.StructureReader

Use absolute imports and explicit relative imports

- In python3 absolute imports are checked first before implicit relative imports
- In python2 this was the other way around, so if your module had a submodule names math, then `import math` would import that submodule rather than the module from the standard library
- Add `from __future__ import absolute_import` to bring this behavior to python2
- Absolute imports used for core python modules
- Submodules imported from q2mm or other python modules should use absolute import syntax or atleast explicit relative syntax
- E.g. `import q2mm.gradient` or `import .gradient` are ok but not `import gradient` when importing q2mm's gradient submodule

Use python3 division to result in float

- In python3, division of two ints results in a float
- In python2, this resulted in an int instead
- Use `from __future__ import division` to bring python3 division behavior to python2
- If you desire the old behavior, use `//` as the division operator to return an int
- I've done some preliminary checks and didn't see any obvious places where the int was needed without explicitly being typed
- If anything breaks, please keep this change in mind if your code uses any division

Changing instances of map() to list comprehension

- In python3 map() now returns an iterator instead of a list
- I've exchanged cases where a list was needed with list comprehensions
- I tried to leave map() in places where an iterator would still work
- In the future use list comprehensions when you need a list, or map
when you need an iterator
- Wrapping map in list (i.e. list(map(func, iterable))) is OK but not
very pythonic

Changing izip() to zip()

- In python3 zip() now generates an iterator where in python2 izip() from itertools was needed to do this.
- Previously I changed these to use zip() if python3 was being used or izip() if python2 was being used
- In favor of readability and removing unnecessary dependencies I've changed all of these to just use zip() regardless of python version
- This is highly unlikely to cause any significant problems with performance

Changing xrange() to range()

- In python3 range() now behave exactly how xrange() did in python2
- Most likely this won't affect performance anywhere, so for readability just using range()

Changing any dict.iter*() to dict.*()

- In python3 dict.iteritems(), dict.iterkeys(), etc. has been removed
- Similarly dict.viewitems(), etc. has also been removed
- Instead dict.items(), etc. now returns a view object
- Views are memory efficient like iterators but are dynamic in that
  changing the dictionary changes what is in the view
- For the most part, when iterating over the keys or values in a dict
  it will work the same as iterating over lists unless the dict object
  is changed

Leaving version switch to deal with basestring

- Basestring has been removed from python3 as all text-type strings
  are now unicode, which was not the case in python2
- Most solutions to this require dependence on `six` or another python
  module for dealing with python2/3 differences in a clean way
- Since most of these compatabilities have been handled without using
  an external dependence then to avoid adding that dependence I'm just
  going to leave the if statements which switch behavior based on
  python version

Corrected mistakes in functioning of SVD

Here is how SVD functions as of this commit.

Let's say we have 2 parameters and 20 data points. The Jacobian is
[20, 2] and the residual vector is [20, 1].

We then used reduced SVD (not full SVD, see the NumPy documentation
for numpy.linalg.svd) on the Jacobian, J = U . s . VT.

Here, U is [20, 2], s is a [2, 1] vector and VT is the transpose of
V, both of which are [2, 2]. In code, this is as so.

mu, vs, mvt = np.linalg.svd(jacob)
ms = np.diag(vs)

We can form the diagonal matrix, ms or S, from vs or s as shown
above. We can also confirm that this method works as intended by
doing the following.

reform = mu.dot(np.diag(vs).dot(mvt))
np.allclose(jacob, reform)

This should return True, indicating that jacob and reform are the
same. This check is now built into the function return_svd, but is
not used by default in order to save time.

We can form the inverted matrix, S', as so.

ms = np.diag(vs)
msi = np.linalg.inv(ms)

In this inverted matrix, msi or S', smaller values come 1st (diagonal
elements increase from index [0, 0] to [n, n] where n is the length
of vector vs).

~~~~~~~~~~

SVD without any modifications is performed to generate trial parameter
changes as such.

X' = VT . S' . UT . r
X' = [2, 2] . [2, 2] . [2, 20] . [20, 1]
X' = [2, 2] . [2, 2] . [2, 1]
X' = [2, 2] . [2, 1]
X' = [2, 1]

Here, X' is the parameter changes and r is the residual vector.

In code, here's what it looks like.

changes = mvt.T.dot(msi.dot(mu.T.dot(resid)))

~~~~~~~~~~

We then modify S' in various way to acquire other trial parameter
changes.

For SVD without thresholds, we zero diagonal elements of S'/msi to
form S", starting with the largest values. A simplified version of
the code looks something like this.

for i in xrange(0, len(vs) - 1):
    msi[-(i + 1), -(i + 1)] = 0.
    changes = mvt.T.dot(msi.dot(mu.T.dot(resid)))

How the torsional check works:
 1. Figure out atom numbers in a torsion.
 2. Break that down into two angles.
 3. Check those angles in the given structure to make sure neither is
    near 180 degrees.
 4. If either is near 180 degrees, exclude this torsion.

The torsional value for a torsion that has an inside angle near 180
degrees can fluctuate wildly. We don't want to include such sensitive,
unstable data in the optimization.

Changed how merges occur

How it worked before:

Common atoms found in structure a and b.
Any missing properties from common atoms in a were copied from b.
Freeze a atoms.
Minimize b atoms.

How it works now (basically the same but with another step):

Common atoms found in structure a and b.
Any missing properties from common atoms in a were copied from b.
Copy coordinates from the common atoms in b into the common atoms in a.
Freeze a atoms.
Minimize b atoms.

Added options to invert Hessian

The Hessian can now be inverted using the command -i somefloat for
calculate. This applies to -jh, -gh, -jeigz, -geigz.

For -jh and -gh, the Hessian is decomposed into its eigenvectors and
eigenvalues using numpy.linalg.eigh, the eigenvalue is inverted, and
the Hessian is reformed.

For -jeigz, we read the Hessian and eigenvectors. This is used to
form the eigenvalue matrix. The diagonal is extracted (all off
diagonal elements should be nearly zero), the lowest value is
inverted, and then the eigenvalue matrix is reformed as a strictly
diagonal matrix.

For -geigz, we simply read the eigenvalues. The lowest value is
inverted, and the eigenvalues are used to form a diagonal matrix.

Added boolean on/off switch for selecting which charges to use.

Now, in the .mae files, you may include an atom property,
"b_q_use_charge". This is a boolean (0 or 1) property. Here's how
it works.

You may use -mq or -jq just like before with the calculate module.
If an atom doesn't have the property "b_q_use_charge" or if the
property "b_q_use_charge" is 1, then the partial charge of that
atom will be considered as a data point. If "b_q_use_charge" is 0,
then that charge is ignored.

This is progress towards issue #7, which raised concerns as to which
partial charges should be included in the optimization. It's now
up to the user to make that decision, and it's very flexible.
The drawback of this method is that it requires the user to edit
their Maestro files (.mae), which may be fairly time consuming.

An alternative method would be to use a separate text file
containing the atom numbers for the atoms whose partial charge
we want to include. I may add this as an option to the calculate
module later.

Another method would be to automatically detect which atoms have
custom dipole parameters by generating a MacroModel (.mmo) file,
but that would require an additional MacroModel calculation in
the case of -jq (if -jq was used alone), and may slow down -mq.
